BACKGROUND

This section surveys the goals, processes, and mechanisms of the PRC’s state-directed industrial planning. Overall, the government at the highest level chooses the individual industries that will receive significant government support, and the provincial and local level governments follow suit. The PRC’s industrial planning begins with the State Council, China’s highest state administrative organ, setting national priorities, then provincial and local level governments following in lockstep in those same industries. That implementation utilizes various mechanisms, including 1) subsidies of various kinds; 2) regulation; 3) guidance funds; and 4) government procurement and SOE coordination. Each mechanism complements the others, creating interwoven threads in the tapestry of PRC state-directed industrial planning.

In the 2020s, the PRC’s centrally planned, command-and-control economy evolved in multiple directions. First, China’s State Council called to move the Chinese economy up the value chain through initiatives such as developing “new quality productive forces.” 10 It sought to indigenize entire supply chains for industries the PRC deems critical, such as aerospace.11 And it has targeted specific industries and products that the PRC deems "chokepoints" to its national security and self-reliance.

CCP General Secretary Xi Jinping himself established the doctrine in April 2020. Speaking to the Central Financial and Economic Affairs Commission, he directed the party to "tighten the dependence of international production chains on our country, forming a powerful capacity for countermeasures and deterrence against artificial supply cutoffs by outside parties" [拉紧国际产业链对我国的依存 关系，形成对外方人为断供的强有力反制和威慑能力]. 12 China should also build "an autonomous, controllable, safe and reliable domestic production and supply system" in fields bearing on national security. 13 That system must be able to "self-circulate" at critical moments, so that "the economy operates normally under extreme circumstances.”14 China should also build "an autonomous, controllable, safe and reliable domestic production and supply system" in fields bearing on national security. 15 That system must be able to "self-circulate" at critical moments, so that "the economy operates normally under extreme circumstances" [在关键时 刻可以做到自我循环，确保在极端情况下经济正常运转].16
The formulation has two halves. Abroad, China wants leverage. At home, it wants autarky. Both halves are borne out in the industries below.

History and Goals of China’s Industrial Planning The modern form of CCP industrial planning originated in the late 1970s, with the “Reform and Opening Up” [改革开放] program. The reforms did not abolish state direction of the industrial structure; instead, they subordinated central planning of prices,17 output, and employment within industries to markets while retaining state authority over the allocation of resources across industries.18 That sequence has three tiers: 1) upgrade traditional industries; 2) scale up emerging industries; and 3) cultivate future industries.19 Around 2006, Chinese industrial policy pivoted from the microeconomic liberalization that had dominated the 1990s and early 2000s back toward assertive state intervention and economic planning. 20 Provincial and local governments deployed subsidies and regulatory measures to re-shape the sectoral composition of the economy and to grow its production of higher-value goods and services. The SOE sector, whose share of industrial output had fallen sharply through the 1990s, resumed a growing role in strategic sectors, both through procurement and as the primary engine of growth in certain industries. Moreover, the party-state began to articulate ambitions to set global technical standards rather than merely absorb foreign ones.21

The current phase crystallized with Made in China 2025 [中国制造2025] (MIC 2025). In 2015, the State Council announced MIC 2025. The program set the objective of transforming the PRC from a “manufacturing great power” [制造大国 ] into a “manufacturing strong power” [制造强国], and ultimately into a selfreliant one, with 2025 as the first waypoint. 22 Premier Li Keqiang framed the underlying problem in 2015 as one of an economy that was “big, but not strong” [ 大而不强]. 23 Xi Jinping’s report to the 19th National Congress of the CCP in October 2017 fixed the aspiration in canonical form: to “promote China’s industries toward the medium-high end of the global value chain, and cultivate a number of world-class advanced manufacturing clusters” [促进我国产业迈向全球 价值链中高端，培育若干世界级先进制造业集群].24

Made in China 2025 used a combination of legacy and novel policy tools (discussed below in greater detail). On the legacy side of the ledger, they included subsidies and regulations. And on the novel side of the ledger, they included SOE procurement, guidance catalogs, and SOE expansion in targeted sectors.

Figure 3 – Graphic of PRC Market Interventions In the mid-2020s, the PRC tripled down on its market-interventionist industrial policy. The party-state set the objective of making the PRC a global leader in technical standards across strategic sectors. It articulated that vision in the National Standardization Development Outline [国家标准化发展纲要] issued jointly by the CCP Central Committee, the top leadership body of the CCP, and the State Council in October 2021, and operationalized in the New-Industry Standardization Pilot Program Implementation Plan (2023–2035) [新产业标准化领 航工程实施方案（2023—2035 年）], issued by the PRC’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) and other departments in August 2023, which targets standards leadership in fields including integrated circuits, high-end machine tools, and biotechnology.25 The PRC has increasingly sought to build self-reliance in “chokepoint” [卡脖子] sectors that produce bottleneck inputs to sectors deemed critical by the PRC. During this same time frame, PRC industrial policy has also seen greater use of export controls, expensing policies, and guidance funds.26

To better understand how China’s state-directed policies operate, some of the different mechanisms used by the Chinese government to implement its state-directed economic priorities are laid out below, although this report will only cover part of the non-market behaviors the PRC uses to strengthen its domestic

- 15 industry. As is well understood, the PRC also uses a variety of tactics aimed at extracting innovation and capital from abroad, such as forcing foreign companies to enter joint ventures with local PRC companies, intellectual property theft, forced technology transfer, and other mechanisms. This report will focus primarily on the affirmative domestic industrial policies that China uses to shape and effectuate its manufacturing priorities.
Mechanisms

Process. The PRC adopts a top-down process to implement its industrial policy. Industrial policy begins at the State Council, which sets nationwide, multi-year targets, identifying the sector for both sectors, quality, and quantity. Sectoral targets cascade through the Five-Year Plans [五年规划], including the Outline of the 14th Five-Year Plan (2021–2025) as well as the Long-Range Objectives Through 2035.27 Provincial and local authorities then implement those initiatives through the mechanisms detailed below. The vertical structure of the system is the source of both its 28 power and its problems: local governments and firms deploy resources to advance their own interests, producing duplicative investment and overcapacity.29 The Chinese government calibrates its market interventions based on the PRC’s level of market dominance. For example, in areas such as industrial chemicals where the PRC already leads, the government provides fewer economic incentives. For other areas such as semiconductors and aerospace, the PRC government lavishes subsidies to spur its domestic industry.

Subsidies. The PRC uses multiple forms of subsidies in its industrial policy. It directly subsidizes industry, which is often disclosed in the financial statements of listed firms. It also uses a series of indirect subsidies, including generous tax-expensing policies for research and development and below-market loans from state banks, and it deploys government guidance funds to subsidize designated sectors. The Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimated that China spent approximately $248 billion—1.73 percent of GDP—on industrial policy in 2019, more than any comparable economy; South Korea, in second place, spent 0.67 percent of GDP, and the United States 0.39 percent.30 On the tax side, the PRC raised the R&D expense additional deduction to 100% (meaning firms can deduct 200% of the R&D value) for eligible firms generally and an additional 120% for integrated-circuit and industrial-mother-machine firms (meaning firms can deduct 220% of the R&D value), allowing such firms to deduct 120% of qualifying R&D expenditure that is expensed, and to amortize 220% of R&D that is capitalized, from 2023 through 2027.31 Additionally, Chinese income tax favors “high and new technology enterprises.” China’s statutory ordinary tax rate is 25%,32 while “high and new technology enterprises” receive a lower rate of 15%.33

Regulation. The PRC party-state possesses greater regulatory capacity than most large economies. The party-state has ultimate control over land, which cannot be “owned” in the American sense but only leased for a long-term period, such as 70 years for residential purposes.34 Those two mechanisms, in conjunction, give the PRC party-state wide latitude to implement regulatory measures: it can allocate inputs, throttle or accelerate approvals, and steer procurement toward favored firms – instruments that operate as subsidies-in-kind without appearing in any budget.35

Guidance Catalogs. The PRC’s industrial policy relies on guidance catalogs, which designate industries and products as encouraged, restricted, or prohibited and thereby channel investment, credit, and administrative approvals. As experts have stated, the catalogs “provide a comprehensive guide to the government’s industrial priorities,” and the way an industry is treated in them strongly shapes that industry’s access to government-controlled resources, including loans from state-owned banks and land for large projects. 36 Guidance catalogs are often enforced through the PRC party-state’s control of land.

SOE Coordination. The PRC uses SOE procurement to re-structure the economy. SOEs, in particular the central ones supervised by the State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission (SASAC) [国务院国有资产监 督管理委员会], function as demand-pull instruments in strategic sectors. Public-sector fleet electrification for new-energy vehicles (EVs) is the paradigmatic example: the State Council’s New Energy Vehicle Industry Development Plan (2021–2035) provides that, “from 2021, in national ecological-civilization pilot zones and key air-pollution-prevention regions, the proportion of new-energy vehicles among newly added or replaced public-domain vehicles, buses, taxis, logistics and delivery vehicles, and the like, shall be not less than 80%” [2021 年起 ，国家生态文明试验区、大气污染防治重点区域的公共领域新增或更新公交、出租 、物流配送等车辆中新能源汽车比例不低于80%].37 By converting a mandated share of state and municipal fleets into guaranteed offtake, the party-state manufactures demand that de-risks capacity expansion by favored producers.38 Guidance Funds. A unique feature of the PRC’s industrial policy is its use of guidance funds. Government guidance funds [政府引导基金] are state-seeded, market-structured investment vehicles: public capital anchors the fund, which is then organized as a private-equity or venture vehicle to invest in designated sectors and to “crowd in” local-government and private co-investment. 39 The flagship is the National Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund [国家集成电 路产业投资基金] (also known as the “Big Fund” [国家大基金]). Its three phases registered RMB 98.72 billion (USD $14.78 billion) against RMB 138.7 billion (USD $20.77 billion) raised (Phase I, September 2014), RMB 204.15 billion (USD $30.57

- 17 billion) (Phase II, October 2019), and RMB 344 billion (USD $51.51 billion) (Phase III, registered May 24, 2024), with the Ministry of Finance as the single largest shareholder. 40 In January 2025, the General Office of the State Council issued Guiding Opinions on Promoting the High-Quality Development of Government Investment Funds, signaling central concern to discipline the proliferation and returns of the guidance-fund model.41
CASE STUDY 1: BIOMANUFACTURING

Biomanufacturing refers to the industry that seeks to harness living systems, such as plant cells or other microorganisms, as industrial factories to generate commercial products. It first appeared in the State Council’s Fifteenth Five-Year plan (covering the years 2026 – 2030).42 China recognized the significant utility associated with this new technology and engaged in a whole-of-society effort utilizing its state-directed industrial planning to rapidly develop and scale up this technology.43 Inclusion in the Fifteenth Five-Year plan signaled top-level government intent to dominate the industry.
I.
Subsidies

Beijing employed the same subsidy architecture used in other critical industries. Mirroring other manufacturing enterprises, biomanufacturing benefits from the R&D super deduction. Moreover, provinces provide significant financial subsidies for building biomanufacturing facilities. The Heilongjiang government offers a full suite of subsidies to enable biomanufacturing across the province.44 For research and development, the Heilongjiang government contributes one-for-one for research and development costs exceeding 500,000 yuan (~$75,000 USD).45 For scaling up manufacturing, Heilongjiang offers a subsidy of up to 10M yuan ($1.5M USD) (30% of the total investment) for pilot-scale manufacturing plants.46 If the facility is designated by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology as a “national biomanufacturing pilot-scale capacity building platform” [生物制造中试能力建设平台], it can be subsidized up to 50%.47 Again, Heilongjiang is not alone. Beijing also offers a series of financial subsidies to move biomanufacturing to the area. Beijing offers to subsidize up to 30% of the fixed asset value of projects (not to exceed 50M yuan ($7.5 million)). 48 Beijing also operates a “services voucher” system that allows qualifying small and medium enterprises to access free analysis, testing, inspection, and equipment from other institutions.49 For enterprises that receive the formal designation of a “national high-tech enterprise,” the Beijing government offers a one-time payment of 100,000 yuan ($15,000) to support research and development efforts.50
II.
Regulatory

Regulation in this sector runs on three tracks. The first is safety regulations that ensure key information for technical development remains within the country. The Regulations on the Administration of Human Genetic Resources [人 类遗传资源管理条例] restrict foreign access to genetic material in the PRC. Limiting access to domestic genetic information in the PRC while simultaneously importing information from abroad provides asymmetric benefits to domestic firms.51 The second track is the designation power itself. MIIT does not merely fund platforms – it lists them. Then it reviews them every three years and adjusts their service-capability star ratings. For example, it may strike a platform for a strain-leakage incident that causes significant economic loss. It also promises to speed project approvals through commitment-and-filing mechanisms. 52 Thus, listing is both a subsidy and a leash. The third track is export controls. The PRC government widened its list of export-controlled technology to include equipment necessary for the sector’s development.

Biomanufacturing draws on the same guidance-fund architecture described above. The seven-department Implementation Opinions on Promoting the Innovative Development of Future Industries direct governments and state capital to deploy angel, venture-guidance, and industry-guidance funds toward future industries.55 State investors have followed. The State Development and Investment Corporation [国投集团] is a central SOE, and it reports investing more than RMB 5 billion in nearly 33 biomanufacturing companies through six market-based funds. Provincial governments have layered their own measures

- 19 on top, with Shanghai, Guangdong, and Heilongjiang each issuing dedicated support policies.56 The pilot-scale capacity building-platform discussed above adds a further channel, instructing provincial authorities to "make good use of first-set and first-batch insurance compensation policies." It also tells them to guide financial institutions and social capital toward platform construction.57 That instruction ties biomanufacturing to the same first-set insurance mechanism that supports machine tools, described below.

At the lower level, local governments created guidance funds to enable investment in the biomanufacturing space. The Shenzhen government created a synthetic biology fund to turbocharge the industry.58 Shortly afterward, the Shenzhen government released a press release directing investment into the biomanufacturing industry.59 Shenzhen is not alone. Guangzhou also created a biomanufacturing government guidance fund for investment in the sector.60 V.
Results

The sector's results support the emphasis. MIIT reports that the biomanufacturing industry reached RMB 1.1 trillion (USD $165 billion) in scale over the 14th Five-Year Plan period. Chinese producers now account for more than 70% of global fermentation-product output. And Chinese applicants file more than 20% of the world's biomanufacturing patent applications.61 Building on China’s existing domination of the chemicals sector, biomanufacturing enables China to generate a lead in the next generation of chemical production technologies. CASE STUDY 2: AEROSPACE

A principal target of the PRC's recent industrial policy is its aerospace sector. The PRC aims to build an indigenous large passenger aircraft [大飞机] through its national champion, the Commercial Aircraft Corporation of China (COMAC). That category comprises two programs. The C919 is a narrow-body aircraft now in service, and the wide-body C929 is currently under development.

The PRC also seeks to indigenize the supply chain required to build large passenger aircraft, including related industries along the supply chain such as engines, avionics, and other related components. In furtherance of that objective, China lavished money on the sector. CSIS identified approximately $49 billion in financing and subsidies through 2020. It projected total support of up to $72.1 billion. That is several times the roughly $22 billion in subsidies the WTO found Airbus received.62
I.
Subsidies

The PRC heavily subsidizes its domestic aerospace industry. Those subsidies fall into two categories: 1) subsidies towards propping up its state champion; and 2) subsidies to indigenize current chokepoints in the supply chain that are necessary to build civilian aircraft. These subsidies came primarily through local and provincial governments.

Consider production first. The state capitalized and repeatedly injected additional funds into COMAC through its central-SOE shareholders. As mentioned above, CSIS estimated subsidies totaling roughly $49 billion but, with the opaque nature of the financial arrangements, it is impossible to determine a firm amount.63 The program also carries formal national status, which adds to its perceived importance by the party-state. It is the large-aircraft special project [大 型飞机重大专项] under the National Medium- and Long-Term Program for Science and Technology Development. That Program directed the state to "master the design, manufacture and systems-integration technologies of large aircraft" [ 掌握大型飞机的设计、制造和系统集成技术].64

Now consider the supply chain. In step with the State Council’s command to focus on the aerospace industry, provinces and local governments implemented policies to spur development, manufacturing, and localization of aerospace technologies. The Pudong area of Shanghai hosts many of the aerospace suppliers critical to COMAC’s success. The area also offered a series of programs targeted at developing the aerospace sector.65 These subsidies were significant.66 For example, Shanghai offered to subsidize 30% of aerospace research and development costs if certain conditions were met. 67 For certifying parts as airworthy, the Shanghai government offers up to 500,000 RMB, approximately $75,000, per certificate.68 For manufacturing, Shanghai offered to subsidize 10% of the total investment in equipment and software to support manufacturing up to 100M RMB, approximately $15M, per project.69 Shanghai was not the only one. Tianjin, another city in China, threw its hat in the ring to become a key area of Chinese commercial aviation development. Tianjin offered significant subsidies to relocate commercial aviation enterprises to the city. Tianjin’s notice specifically targets projects that address key chokepoints in the aerospace industry and rewards these enterprises with subsidies of 10% of investment up to 5M RMB of investment or approximately $750,000. 70 For companies that received central government certificates, Tianjin would pay a one-time subsidy of 2M RMB or approximately $300,000.71 These subsidies had a significant impact. Airbus built its first final assembly line (FAL) outside of France in Tianjin, delivering its first aircraft in 2009.72 These facilities continued to expand. As shown in the satellite photo below taken in 2026, Airbus’ Tianjin facilities now cover such a wide area that they are easily visible from space.

II.
Regulatory

The PRC has used regulatory barriers to help indigenize its aerospace industry. Various actors in the PRC party-state noted the strategic risk of relying on foreign aircraft. They frame indigenization in national-security and self-reliance terms. The same logic animates the megaproject designation. 78 The Chinese state wielded regulatory barriers to facilitate technology transfer, expedite adoption of domestically produced aircraft, and enable foreign certification of Chinese aircraft.

First, regulatory barriers enable technology transfer. As part of its administrative and licensing process, the PRC requires disclosure of sensitive aerospace technology.79 This review occurs both at the central government level and the local provincial level.80 Uncertainty about the applicable rules provides Chinese authorities with wide discretion to use administrative processes to pressure non-PRC companies to relinquish technology, restrict investments to protect domestic competitors, or otherwise act in furtherance of industrial policy objectives.81 One legal treatise on foreign investment in the PRC stated that a Catalogue of Industries for Encouraging Foreign Investment82 allows a wholly owned foreign entity to operate in a sector, but the Chinese authorities openly state they require a joint venture in the same sector.83 Airworthiness certification by the Civil Aviation Administration of China (CAAC) cuts both ways. It supplied the C919 domestic type certificate in September 2022, and the first delivery occurred in December 2022. Entry into service followed in May 2023. But certification and delivery decisions for foreign types are also available as leverage. China grounded the Boeing 737 MAX in March 2019. Its commercial service did not resume until January 2023. Boeing deliveries were paused again amid trade tensions in 2024 and 2025.84 Market access has served the same end. Joint-venture requirements and offsets were historically used to extract technology transfer into the PRC aviation supply chain.85 More recently, in 2026, China delayed final approvals of Airbus aircraft to pressure the European Union Aviation Safety Agency to approve the COMAC C919.86
III.
SOE Coordination

The PRC has used its SOEs' significant purchasing power to indigenize its supply chain. Air China [中国国际航空], China Eastern [中国东方航空], and China Southern [中国南方航空] are all state carriers. Each announced a firm order for 100 C919 aircraft, with deliveries scheduled from 2024 through 2031. 87 Industry observers described the purchase order process for C919 as “state directed,” “coerced,” and “choreographed” by the PRC government.88 Aircraft purchases require PRC government approval.89 China uses this leverage to balance purchases of foreign aircraft and to pressure Western firms to form joint ventures with Chinese firms to localize production.90 Additionally, China used its SOE airlines to coordinate purchases of aircraft from “strategic partners,”91 specifically Airbus. In the market for large wide-body aircraft, there are two market leaders: Boeing and Airbus. While Boeing made certain limited investments in China, Airbus bent over backwards for the CCP. China is Airbus’ largest sales market.92 Airbus opened several sprawling facilities in China, including its first A320 FAL outside Europe in Tianjin as described above. Airbus also opened an airplane-recycling facility in Chengdu,93 an A330 finishing facility in Tianjin (its first outside of Europe94) and a FAL for the H135 helicopter in Qingdao.95 Beyond these facilities, Airbus invested in the Chinese aerospace technical ecosystem. Airbus opened a research and development center in Suzhou.96 It also opened an innovation center in Shenzhen to “[access] a highly advanced digital innovation ecosystem.”97 In return for Airbus selling its capabilities and know-how, China rewarded it handsomely. As mentioned above, China is Airbus’s largest country market. While Boeing has not received a major Chinese aircraft order since 2017,98 Airbus continues to see significant orders from Chinese state-owned carriers. In tandem with these subsidies, regulatory measures, and SOE purchase agreements, the Chinese government created a series of government guidance funds to turbocharge the aerospace industry. CASE STUDY 3: SEMICONDUCTORS

China’s semiconductor strategy is among the most critical, and most discussed, elements of the broader technological and economic competition. 112 While semiconductors with small-nanometer transistors that power leading-edge computing are also central to U.S. national and economic security, this section focuses on the PRC’s strategy to dominate foundational-node or “legacy” semiconductors. The PRC has concentrated its financial firepower on mature (“foundational”) nodes of 28nm and above, which power consumer-grade electronics that do not require high computing power, such as automotive controllers, power management, displays, and image sensors. Because of foundational models’ essential role in cars, consumer electronics, and other manufactured products, they constitute a chokepoint input.

China released a semiconductor strategy to provide a comprehensive plan for meeting the country’s semiconductor objectives.113 This document called for the rapid expansion of China’s integrated circuit production capacity, specifically calling out production at nodes in the 45/40 nanometer (nm) range, 32/28 nm range.114 As described below, the 2020 policy kicked off significant subsidy efforts by local and provincial governments to turbocharge the semiconductor industry. I.
Subsidies

The PRC provides generous tax relief for semiconductor producers. In 2020, the State Council announced tiered corporate-income-tax relief tied to manufacturing capabilities [国发〔2020〕8 号]. The operative language provides: "For state-encouraged integrated-circuit manufacturing enterprises or projects with a line width smaller than 28nm (inclusive) and an operating period of more than 15 years, enterprise income tax shall be exempted from the first year through the tenth year" [国家鼓励的集成电路线宽小于28 纳米（含），且经营期在15 年以 上的集成电路生产企业或项目，第一年至第十年免征企业所得税]. Firms at 65nm and below with a 15-year horizon receive five years' exemption plus five years at half the statutory 25% rate. Firms at 130nm and below with a 10-year horizon receive two years' exemption plus three years at half rate [两免三减半].

The relief thus was not limited to leading-edge producers. It extended to producers of foundational semiconductor nodes. The same policy provided import-duty relief for inputs necessary to produce semiconductors with transistors smaller than 65 nanometers. And the policy was implemented across the provinces. Provincial tax administrations issued their own documents implementing the schedule.115

On top of corporate tax relief, the PRC offered semiconductor manufacturers generous tax deductions. The most significant is the 120% research-and-development super-deduction. It provides that "the research and development expenses actually incurred by integrated-circuit enterprises and industrial-mother-machine enterprises … shall, from January 1, 2023 to December 31, 2027, be additionally deducted before tax at 120% of the amount actually incurred" [集 成电路企业和工业母机企业……在2023 年1 月1 日至2027 年12 月31 日期间，再 按照实际发生额的120% 在税前扣除]. Capitalized research draws a 220% amortization allowance. 116 A parallel 5% value-added-tax super-credit for advanced-manufacturing enterprises supplements the income-tax measures.117 All of these provisions operate as a subsidy on the industry because they enable different companies to collect money exceeding their expenditures. At the provincial and local levels, government officials began to roll out schemes providing additional economic benefits to semiconductor firms that moved to their geographic area. Jiangsu province announced a program to sponsor national-level technology innovation centers with up to 30M RMB, or roughly $4.4M, and national-level manufacturing centers receiving no less than 30M RMB.118 The city of Hefei provided subsidies for companies that purchased local equipment from local integrated circuit and packaging companies.119 II.
Regulatory

The PRC uses a wide array of regulatory tools to indigenize its semiconductor sector. The below lays out the timeline of tightening restrictions China placed on foreign integrated circuits in its market.

First, the PRC has sharply limited the importation of foreign-made semiconductors, to cultivate its domestic production. In one government announcement, the PRC claimed that American-made semiconductors had serious network-security defects. The Cyberspace Administration of China's cybersecurity review of May 21, 2023 falsely found that Micron's products "have relatively serious potential network-security problems." Those problems, it said, posed a major risk to critical-information-infrastructure supply chains.
It therefore directed that "operators of critical information infrastructure shall stop purchasing Micron's products" [存在较严重网络安全问题隐患……国内关键 信息基础设施的运营者应停止采购美光公司产品].120

China increased the pressure in March 2024 when it issued guidelines requiring the phaseout of Intel and AMD microprocessors from government computers.121 The notice required PRC government agencies above the township level to buy “safe and reliable” processors and operating systems.122 All companies meeting the criteria were Chinese.123 The CCP also ratcheted up the pressure by purportedly issuing "Document 79" [79 号文, 2022], which directed state firms to replace foreign hardware and software by 2027 under the xinchuang [ 信创] program.124

With the government market closed off, China set out to bring commercial industry to heel. In April 2024, the PRC government directed telecommunications firms to phase out foreign chips that are key to their networks by 2027. 125 In December 2024, four PRC industry associations jointly misled members that U.S. chip products are "no longer safe, no longer reliable" [不再安全、不再可靠].126 They counseled caution in procurement.127 In parallel, the Internet Society of China urged domestic Chinese companies to think carefully before procuring U.S. chips and instead seek to expand cooperation with firms from countries or regions other than the United States.128

In a move to increase pressure on foreign foundational node chips, in January 2025, China’s Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) opened an investigation into U.S.-origin mature-node analog chips to determine whether they harmed PRC industry.129 In opening the investigation, MOFCOM cited the CHIPS and Science Act’s subsidies and claimed they gave American firms an “unfair advantage.”130 MOFCOM’s statement conveniently left out the plethora of subsidies given to Chinese firms. MOFCOM followed this inquiry with an anti-dumping investigation into American IC chips announced in September 2025.131 This nearconstant pressure did not end.

In early 2026, the U.S. government approved the sale of NVIDIA’s H200 chips for export to China.132 According to a report, the U.S. approved the sale of H200 chips to multiple Chinese firms including Alibaba, Tencent, and JD.com. 133 However, the PRC government refused the H200 chips, instead pushing its own homegrown industry.134
The above series of events shows the constant regulatory pressure China applies to manufacture demand for its indigenous chipmakers. Beginning in May
2023 and continuing until the present, the Chinese government applied nearconstant pressure on the government and domestic industry to buy Chinese chips. III.
SOE Coordination

The PRC uses its large public sector as a means of expanding its semiconductor industry. This is largely through the SOEs' significant purchasing power. For instance, PRC telecommunications carriers, which are all SOEs, promulgated new procurement guidelines requiring domestic chips. The three state carriers, China Mobile, China Telecom, and China Unicom, [中国移动, 中国电信, 中国联通] award scoring bonuses in centralized-procurement [集采] tenders to domestic processors and "safe and reliable" platforms. They reportedly face directives to phase foreign-core chips out of their networks by 2027. And they increasingly reserve servertender lots for domestically designed CPUs [鲲鹏, 海光, 飞腾].135 SOE demand-pull thereby absorbs the mature-node capacity that state subsidy has built. That closes the loop between supply-side subsidy and demand-side procurement.
IV.
Guidance Funds

The PRC has aggressively subsidized the manufacturing of legacy semiconductor nodes. This is primarily through its "Big Funds" [国家集成电路产 业投资基金]. The Big Funds invest in PRC semiconductor firms, often in exchange for equity and control. Big Fund capital has grown across three phases. Phase I raised RMB 138.7 billion (USD $20.8 billion) in 2014. Phase II raised RMB 204.15 billion (USD $30.61 billion) in 2019. Phase III registered RMB 344 billion (USD $51.57 billion) in 2024. Analysts estimate that Phase III alone could mobilize on the order of RMB 1.5 trillion (USD $225 billion) once local-government and social co-investment is levered in.
136 Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (SMIC) [中芯国际] and Hua Hong Semiconductor are among the Fund's principal portfolio companies.137 V.
Results

China’s aggressive push into this node of the semiconductor supply chain is unfair to international firms, but it is working. The PRC’s aggressive industrial policy towards semiconductors has increased its share of global mature-node foundry capacity from 29–31% in 2023 to 34% in 2024, second to Taiwan’s 43%.138 TrendForce projects “China’s breakneck expansion is expected to propel it past Taiwan by 2027,” with the PRC reaching approximately 47% of mature-node capacity and Taiwan falling to about 36%.139 The PRC’s national integrated-circuit output reached 451.4 billion units in 2024, up 22.2% year-on-year. 140
Semiconductor Equipment and Materials International (SEMI), a leading

- 29 semiconductor trade organization, counts 57 of the 97 new fabs slated to begin operation worldwide between 2023 and 2025 as located in the PRC.141 The trajectory of SMIC, China’s national foundry champion, illustrates the pattern. For full-year 2025, SMIC reported revenue of US$9.33 billion (up 16.2% from US$8.03 billion in 2024, which itself was up 27%), a gross margin of 21.0% (recovered from 18.0% in 2024 but well below the 30.8% of 2022), capacity utilization of 93.5% (up roughly eight points from 85.6%), capital expenditure of roughly US$7.3–8.1 billion per year, and monthly capacity exceeding 1,059,000 8-inch-equivalent wafers, up from 948,000, an increase of roughly 111,000 wafers per month over the prior year.142 The company is running four simultaneous mature-node fab projects (中芯京城 in Beijing, 中芯东方 in Shanghai’s Lingang, 中芯西青 in Tianjin, and 中芯深圳 in Shenzhen).

So far, the PRC’s semiconductor industrial policy is largely defensive. It seeks to protect and subsidize its domestic industry to reduce foreign reliance. But the line between its defensive and offensive posture is a thin one. The more the PRC obtains global production capacity in foundational semiconductors, the greater control it has over the global supply chain of this node. This supply chain is essential to many consumer electronics. As a result, the PRC’s creeping control presents a risk to the economic interests of the United States and its allies. CASE STUDY 4: MACHINE TOOLS

The PRC has designated machine tools the "industrial mother machines" [工 业母机/工作母机]. They comprise the capital equipment that makes all other manufacturing equipment. The CCP elevated high-end computer-numerical-control (CNC) machine tools [高档数控机床] to explicit chokepoint status. It listed them among the top ten priority fields of Made in China 2025. And it funded them through the "04 Special Project" [04 专项], one of the sixteen national science-and-technology megaprojects under the 2006 Program.143 The PRC specifically frames the importance of “industrial mother machines,” a term used by the CCP to describe machine tools, as a key part of its military modernization.144 CNC machines play an important role in the machining of industrial components. 145 CNC machines enable precision milling, drilling, and cutting operations at high volumes. 146 The PRC is the world's largest producer and consumer of machine tools.147

The PRC is especially sensitive to the chokepoint nature of the machine tool sector. SASAC and the party leadership have repeatedly listed “ 工业母机” (industrial mother machines) first among the fields requiring breakthroughs in
- 30 key core technologies. 148 Placing this field first signals its importance to PRC industrial policy.
I.
Subsidies

The sector draws significant state subsidies to turbocharge it. These funds can be grouped into project funds, tax policies, and insurance subsidies. The first is 04-project money. The PRC State Council’s creation of Project 4 identified it as a key priority area, thus unlocking additional funding.149 Moreover, identifying this area as a project signals to the local governments that they should follow suit in their subsidies for CNC machining equipment. For example, the Changzhou government provides an additional subsidy of 20% of the special state support funds, up to a maximum of 3 million yuan for companies participating in a major national science and technology project.150 The third is the tax code. At the central government level, the 120% research-and-development super-deduction covers industrial-mother-machine enterprises by its own terms, alongside integrated-circuit firms.151 Moreover, high-end CNC machine companies qualify as “high and new technology enterprises” meaning the government applies the lower 15% rate.152
II.
Regulatory

China’s preference for domestically produced CNC machines dates back to at least 2015. In 2015, China recognized that businesses are hesitant to adopt expensive products that lack a track record, which would inhibit development of its own domestic industry. To solve this issue, the PRC launched a state-sponsored insurance plan that provides initial customers of certain newly developed products, such as CNC machines, with quality- and liability-related risk insurance.153 This program remains active as of this report.154 To complement this insurance scheme, China implemented a demand-side specific policy in 2017 as part of its Military-Civil Fusion Special Action Plan.155 This Action Plan called for greater application of high-end CNC machines in China’s military industry as well as a host of policies to favor domestically produced CNC machines. 156 In 2018, the Chinese government expanded this policy by launching a whole-of-government approach to spurring the domestic CNC machine industry.157 The policy called on multiple bureaus such as the State Taxation Administration, the National Development and Reform Commission, the National Health Commission, and the State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission of the State Council to coordinate policy that would spur the research, development, and adoption of domestically produced CNC machines. 158 Overall, these policies push domestic companies to purchase domestically produced CNC machines to spur China’s domestic industry.
III.
SOE Coordination

China treats CNC machines as strategic core assets and thus maintains significant control over the industry. This strategic importance dates to the early days of the PRC. In 1953, the First Ministry of Machine Building created 18 machine tool factories that became known as the “Eighteen Arhats” of the PRC’s machine tool industry.159 Even though the PRC later privatized many businesses, most of the largest CNC machine manufacturers are still SOEs. For example, the China General Technology Group (Genertec, [中国通用技术集团] is the dominant SOE that treats machine tools as a core business. It absorbed the bankrupt Shenyang Machine Tool [沈阳机床], whose reorganization was completed in December 2019. Genertec also absorbed Dalian Machine Tool [大连机床]. And it thereby gathered several of the "Eighteen Arhats" under one roof.160 SASAC and Genertec's leadership styled the group as the machine-tool industry's "national team" [国家队]. The group pledged to "unswervingly make the development of high-end machine-tool equipment its first core main business" [坚定不移把发展高 端机床装备作为第一核心主业].161

Chinese CNC machine companies then sell to other state-owned Chinese companies to prop up their business. For example, Kede Numerical Control Co., ltd. (Kede) [科德数控股份有限公司] notes that its largest customers are Chinese SOEs such as AVIC, the Aeroengine Corporation of China, and the China State Shipbuilding Corporation (the predecessor to the state-owned China Shipbuilding Industry Company). 162 Shenyang Machine Tool Company (Shenyang Machine Tool) counts business with AVIC subsidiaries and Genertec as providing more than 70% of its operating revenue in 2023.163 Qinchuan Machine Tool Group, [秦川机床工具集团股份公司], another state-owned machine tool company, relies on major sales to the Shanghai Aircraft Manufacturing
Company

Ltd. supplies Chinese state-owned firms such as Shenyang Liming Aerospace. 165 This coordinated effort ensures CNC machine manufactures have adequate customer demand to deploy and test their products to iterate for the larger marketplace. IV.
Guidance Funds

The machine tools industry is so important to the Party-State that the Chinese government created the National Manufacturing Transformation and Upgrading Fund [国家制造业转型升级基金] and funded it with 15 billion yuan.166 This central government guidance fund is supplemented by local guidance funds such as the

V.
Results

PRC firms dominate low-range and mid-range CNC equipment but remain import-dependent on high-end CNC.169 For low-end CNC equipment, domestic localization reached essentially 100%. 170 For mid-range CNC equipment, the localization rate of mid-range CNC machine tools increased from 62.6% to 73.5%.171 Domestic localization of high-end CNC sat in the low single digits for years. It rose from roughly 2% to 6% between 2013 and 2017, before more recent gains.172 According to a 2024 report from the Chinese government, Project No. 4 increased the domestic market share of high-end CNC machines to over 30%.173 Two important ramifications follow for the United States and its allies. The overcapacity that signals domestic inefficiency also creates both the incentive and the means for China to dump abroad. And chokepoint dominance built for defensive autarky doubles as offensive leverage, as the critical-minerals controls of 2024 and 2025 showed.
IMPLICATIONS FOR U.S. POLICY

As these case studies demonstrate, the PRC’s command-and-control economic model is deliberately built through sustained government intervention, coordinated investment, protected demand, and control over strategic supply chains. Across sectors, Beijing has used these tools to reduce the PRC’s dependence on foreign suppliers while expanding the world’s dependence on Chinese production. The CCP has not achieved technological leadership in every sector, but its ability to mobilize capital, build capacity at scale, and sustain investment over long time horizons presents a significant challenge to U.S. manufacturing capacity and national security.

The implications for U.S. policy are clear. The United States must rebuild critical industrial capabilities that have been lost over decades. A durable response requires a coordinated industrial strategy that treats productive capacity, resilient supply chains, technological leadership, and a skilled workforce as strategic national assets.

Recognizing that the PRC’s state-directed industrial planning poses an existential threat to American industry and technical leadership, the United States must take immediate action. That action should be the formulation and execution of a deliberate industrial strategy to identify key U.S. industries, revitalize them,

- 33 and help defend them against unfair competition from China.
